expl: The original two mappings both describe GET requests against /products/<single segment>, and Spring's mapping matcher only looks at the pattern's structure and HTTP method -- the placeholder names {id} and {productId} are irrelevant to matching, so the two are genuinely identical from the router's point of view, causing the ambiguous-mapping startup failure. Adding a distinguishing literal segment, /products/{id}/details, changes the actual pattern shape (two segments instead of one after /products/), so the two mappings are no longer ambiguous -- GET /products/42 routes to getProduct, and GET /products/42/details routes to getProductDetails, each unambiguously.

exp: GET /search with no query string calls productService.findAll(), because category is not provided and required=false lets the request through with category bound to null, taking the if-branch. GET /search?category=shoes calls productService.findByCategory("shoes"), because category is now bound to the string "shoes", which is not null, so the if-branch is skipped.
expl: Because category is declared @RequestParam(required = false) and there is no defaultValue, an omitted category query parameter does not cause a 400 error -- it simply leaves category bound to null (String is a reference type, so 'absent' naturally maps to null rather than a primitive default). The method's own if (category == null) check then explicitly branches to productService.findAll() for that case. When category=shoes is supplied in the query string, Spring binds the literal string "shoes" to the parameter, category is no longer null, and the method falls through to productService.findByCategory("shoes") instead -- the routing itself is identical in both calls (both hit the same search method); only the bound parameter's value, and therefore the method's own internal branching, differs.

inStock is declared as a Java boolean, but the client sent the JSON string "yes" for it. Jackson's boolean deserializer only accepts the literal JSON values true/false, or the strings "true"/"false" (case-insensitively) -- "yes" is not a recognized boolean representation, so Jackson throws InvalidFormatException while trying to convert the request body into a ProductRequest object. Spring MVC wraps that into HttpMessageNotReadableException, which is automatically translated into a 400 Bad Request response -- and because the ProductRequest object was never successfully constructed, createProduct's method body never runs at all; the failure happens entirely during argument resolution, one layer before the controller code learners often go looking for the bug in. Sending the JSON boolean literal true (not the string "yes") for inStock resolves the type mismatch and lets deserialization -- and the request -- succeed.

exp: 200 OK, with the response body 'Order for: null'. The JSON is syntactically valid and 'custName' doesn't cause an error because Spring Boot's Jackson autoconfiguration disables FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES by default -- an unrecognized key is simply ignored rather than rejected. Since no key in the payload matches customerName, that field is never set and defaults to null, so request.getCustomerName() returns null and the concatenated string is 'Order for: null'.
expl: "custName" is valid JSON and doesn't correspond to any declared property on CreateOrderRequest, but Spring Boot's Jackson configuration explicitly disables the FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES feature (unlike plain, non-Boot Jackson, which enables it by default), so an unrecognized key like this is silently ignored rather than causing an exception. Because customerName was never populated by any key in this particular payload, it keeps its default value of null once the object is constructed -- there is no error at any point, deserialization succeeds completely, and createOrder's body runs normally, concatenating null into the returned string. The response is a perfectly ordinary 200 OK with the body "Order for: null", which is exactly the kind of silent, hard-to-notice bug that field-level validation (@NotBlank, in the next concept) is designed to catch.

@NotBlank rejects a null, empty, or all-whitespace email, and @Email additionally checks that whatever non-blank value IS supplied actually looks like a valid email address -- the two are complementary, not redundant, since @Email alone would not reject a blank string outright in every validator configuration, and @NotBlank alone says nothing about the value's shape. @Min(1) on quantity rejects zero, negative values, and (implicitly, since it's a primitive int) never has to worry about null. None of these annotations do anything by themselves, though -- Bean Validation only actually runs against the constructed SubscriptionRequest object because @Valid was added to the @RequestBody parameter in the controller method; without it, the constraints would sit there, fully valid Java, and simply never be checked, letting invalid requests reach subscribe's body unfiltered.

Plain @ControllerAdvice does not carry @ResponseBody the way @RestControllerAdvice does -- it is built on the same base as plain @Controller, whose return-value handling is oriented around resolving views, not writing a body directly. A return type like Map that isn't a recognized view-related type and isn't explicitly told to be treated as a response body doesn't automatically get serialized to JSON the way it would from an @RestController -- clients end up NOT receiving the clean structured error body the team intended, instead of a helpful error response, undermining the whole point of centralizing error handling in the first place. Switching the class annotation to @RestControllerAdvice (or, equivalently, keeping @ControllerAdvice but adding @ResponseBody directly on handleNotFound) tells Spring MVC to treat this method's return value exactly like an @RestController method would: write it straight to the response body through the registered HttpMessageConverter chain, producing the intended JSON error response.

code:

server.port=8080

# Startup command:
# java -jar app.jar --server.port=9090
expl: Both the command-line argument and the properties file register a value for the same key, server.port, as two separate PropertySources inside the application's single Environment. Command-line arguments sit at the top of Spring Boot's precedence order, above application.properties, so when anything -- in this case, the autoconfiguration responsible for the embedded server -- asks the Environment for server.port, it returns the first value found while walking sources in precedence order, which is the command-line argument's 9090. application.properties's own value of 8080 is never actually consulted for this particular run; the file itself is completely unchanged, and starting the same jar again WITHOUT the --server.port argument would correctly fall back to reading 8080 from the file, since nothing above it in precedence would define the key in that case.

expl: In the buggy version, notifications: has no keys indented further than itself -- retry-count and channel sit at the SAME indentation level as notifications, which YAML interprets as them being siblings of notifications under app, not children of it. That silently produces a property path of app.retry-count (not app.notifications.retry-count), which @ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "app.notifications") never looks at, so its retryCount field is left at whatever default was set in the Java class, 1 -- with no parsing error anywhere, since app.retry-count is itself perfectly valid YAML, just bound to the wrong logical location. Indenting retry-count and channel two spaces further than notifications makes them genuinely nest underneath it, producing the intended app.notifications.retry-count path that the @ConfigurationProperties class is actually configured to read from.

exp: Scenario A starts normally, with cronExpression bound to '0 0 * * * *'. Scenario B fails to start with IllegalArgumentException: Could not resolve placeholder 'app.reports.cron-expression', because the property has no value anywhere in the Environment and the @Value expression supplies no default to fall back on.
expl: The placeholder ${app.reports.cron-expression} has no colon-separated default value written into it, which specifically means Spring has no fallback to use if the real property is missing. In Scenario A, app.reports.cron-expression is defined in application.properties, so the Environment resolves it successfully and ReportScheduler is constructed normally with cronExpression set to the configured cron string. In Scenario B, no property source defines that key at all, and because there's no default to fall back to, Spring MVC's placeholder resolution throws IllegalArgumentException while trying to construct ReportScheduler, which fails the entire application startup rather than silently leaving cronExpression as null. This is the fail-fast behavior that only exists for @Value placeholders WITHOUT a default -- adding one (e.g., :0 0 * * * *) would change Scenario B's outcome to a silent, always-used default instead of a startup failure.

expl: application-prod.properties is loaded as a layered overlay on top of application.properties, not a wholesale replacement -- so every key present in the base file remains in effect unless the profile-specific file also defines that same key. spring.jpa.show-sql and app.max-upload-mb are both defined in application-prod.properties, so their profile-specific values (false and 25) take precedence over the base file's (true and 10). app.support-email has no entry anywhere in application-prod.properties at all, so there's nothing to override its base-file value with -- it resolves to support@example.com exactly as defined in the base file, completely unaffected by which profile is active.

With SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=dev,prod, both dev and prod are simultaneously active, which makes BOTH @Profile("dev") LoggingNotifier and @Profile("prod") SesNotifier eligible for registration at the same time -- both implement Notifier, and with no @Primary or @Qualifier to disambiguate between them, Spring cannot decide which one to inject wherever a Notifier is required, so it refuses to start the application with NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException, naming both conflicting beans. The Java code and its @Profile annotations are correct as written; they were specifically designed to be mutually exclusive, environment-specific alternatives, not beans meant to coexist. The actual bug is the leftover CI configuration activating both profiles together -- correcting SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE to name only dev (the profile actually appropriate for an integration test run) resolves the ambiguity, since only LoggingNotifier's guarding profile is active at that point.

expl: The original OrderService relies on Spring's container to reflectively populate its @Autowired field after construction -- but the test calls `new OrderService()` directly, bypassing Spring entirely, so `notifier` is never set and stays null, causing the NullPointerException on `notifier.send(...)`. Switching to constructor injection removes the dependency on a container altogether: the constructor's signature itself requires a Notifier argument, so `new OrderService(fakeNotifier)` supplies it directly and explicitly, with the exact same code working identically whether Spring is running or not. This is precisely why constructor injection is considered more testable than field injection -- it doesn't merely make tests shorter, it makes plain object construction actually possible.

exp: The application fails to start, throwing a NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException that reports two matching beans for the Shipper type (groundShipper and airShipper) and no way to choose between them.
expl: Both GroundShipper and AirShipper are registered as beans implementing Shipper, and ShippingService's constructor asks for exactly one Shipper. With two equally valid, undistinguished candidates and no @Primary marking a default or @Qualifier naming a specific one at the injection point, Spring cannot decide which bean to pass in, and rather than arbitrarily picking one, it fails the entire application startup with NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException, naming both conflicting candidates in the exception message. Fixing this requires disambiguation -- adding @Primary to whichever Shipper should be the default, or @Qualifier("groundShipper") on the constructor parameter to pick one explicitly.

exp: 'dark' then 'true'. Settings has no explicit @Scope, so it defaults to singleton -- there is exactly one Settings instance in this context. Both `a` and `b` are references to that same single object, so mutating it through `a` is visible through `b`, and `a == b` is true because they are literally the same object, not two equal-but-separate ones.
expl: Because no @Scope is declared on Settings, Spring registers it with the default singleton scope, meaning the container constructs exactly one instance for its entire lifetime and hands that same instance out to every caller of getBean(Settings.class) (and to every other bean that has it injected). `a.setTheme("dark")` mutates that one shared object's theme field. When `b` is obtained via a second getBean(Settings.class) call, it does not get a new, independently-"light"-themed object -- it gets a reference to the very same instance `a` already mutated, so b.getTheme() reports "dark", and a == b evaluates to true because both variables hold references to the identical object in memory, not merely two objects with equal field values.

expl: JacksonConfig was missing @Configuration (or any stereotype annotation at all), so it was never discovered by component scanning and never registered as a bean itself -- which means Spring never calls its objectMapper() method as a bean-producing factory method; the class is entirely inert, just an unused plain Java class sitting in the package. Because no custom ObjectMapper bean is ever actually registered, JacksonAutoConfiguration's own default ObjectMapper bean -- guarded by @ConditionalOnMissingBean(ObjectMapper.class) -- finds that its 'missing bean' condition IS satisfied (there really is no ObjectMapper bean, custom or otherwise) and registers its standard default instead, with none of the intended date-format or module customization. Adding @Configuration makes JacksonConfig itself a bean, which makes its @Bean method a real factory method Spring actually invokes, which registers the custom ObjectMapper and correctly causes the autoconfigured default to back off.

exp: The application now listens on port 8081. The embedded server's autoconfiguration builds its server factory bean using values read from a ServerProperties object (a @ConfigurationProperties class) that is automatically bound from Spring Boot's Environment abstraction, which in turn reads application.properties as one of its sources -- so changing the file changes the bound value the autoconfiguration class consumes, with zero code changes needed.
code:
# application.properties
server.port=8081
expl: The embedded server's autoconfiguration class never hardcodes a port number; instead, it constructs the embedded server factory using a ServerProperties object, whose fields (including port) are automatically populated ('bound') from Spring Boot's Environment abstraction at startup. The Environment merges configuration from multiple sources -- application.properties among them -- into one unified view, with a defined precedence order across sources. Adding server.port=8081 to application.properties adds a value to one of those sources, which changes what ServerProperties.getPort() returns the next time the application starts, which changes what port value the autoconfiguration class passes when building the actual embedded server. No Java source was touched or recompiled -- the same autoconfiguration code ran, and simply read a different value out of the environment this time.

The original getOrder is @Transactional(readOnly = true), so its persistence context closes the instant it returns -- the Order handed to the controller is already detached before ship(...) ever mutates it. Setting order.setStatus(...) in the controller is a plain, untracked field write: no snapshot exists to compare against, no flush is scheduled, and nothing persists, with no error raised anywhere to reveal the problem. The fix adds a dedicated markShipped method, itself @Transactional, that loads the order and mutates it within one single transaction -- so the entity is still managed at the exact moment its status changes, and Hibernate's automatic dirty checking picks up the change and flushes an UPDATE at commit. The controller now delegates the whole fetch-and-mutate operation to that one transactional method instead of pulling a managed entity out of its transaction and mutating it afterward.

exp: true, then SHIPPED. Both findById calls happen inside the same transaction, so they share one persistence context's identity map -- the second lookup for the same id returns the exact same managed object as the first, not a freshly re-read copy. Because first and second are the same object, mutating status through first is immediately visible when reading it through second.
expl: Both calls to orderRepository.findById(orderId) execute within the same @Transactional method, so they operate against the same persistence context. The first call loads the entity and registers it in that context's identity map, keyed by id. The second call, for the same id, does not issue a second independent load that produces a second object -- the persistence context recognizes it already has a managed entity for that id and simply returns the same reference. So `first == second` prints true: they are not merely equal-by-value, they are the identical object in memory. Because of that, first.setStatus(OrderStatus.SHIPPED) mutates the one and only Order object both variables point to, so reading second.getStatus() immediately afterward reports SHIPPED -- there was never a second object to have gone stale.

findByEmail tells Spring Data JPA to generate a query filtering on a property literally named email -- but Order's actual field is customerEmail, so there is no property named email anywhere on the entity's mapped model at all. Spring Data JPA discovers this mismatch while building the repository proxy at startup, before any request is ever served, and fails the whole application with PropertyReferenceException naming the unresolved property. Renaming the method to findByCustomerEmail makes the property segment of the method name match Order's real field exactly; the parameter name (email) is irrelevant to this resolution step -- only the property name embedded in the method name itself has to correspond to a real, mapped property, and once it does, the proxy builds successfully and the method works as intended.

The derived method name is parsed piece by piece: findBy establishes a query, CustomerEmail matches the customerEmail property with equality, And joins a second condition, TotalGreaterThan matches the total property with a > comparison, and OrderByTotalDesc sorts results by total descending -- every piece of vocabulary in the name maps directly onto a clause in the generated query, and Spring Data JPA validates each property name (customerEmail, total) against Order's mapped fields at startup. The JPQL version expresses exactly the same logic explicitly: it selects Order entities, filters on the same two properties using named parameters bound via @Param, and sorts with an ordinary 'order by' clause -- readable as a single query string rather than assembled from name-parsing vocabulary, which becomes the more maintainable choice once a query like this needs to grow any further (an additional join, an OR condition, a subquery) than a derived method name can comfortably express.

exp: 201 queries total: 1 for findAll() plus 1 more for each of the 200 authors, because author.getBooks() is a LAZY collection that only gets fetched with its own separate query the moment .size() is called on it, independently for every author in the loop.
expl: findAll() issues exactly one SELECT that returns all 200 Author rows, with each author's books collection populated as an unfetched LAZY proxy -- no Book rows have been read at that point. The loop then calls author.getBooks().size() once per author; because @OneToMany defaults to LAZY, each of those calls independently triggers Hibernate to resolve that specific author's proxy with its own SELECT ... FROM books WHERE author_id = ? -- 200 separate queries, one per author, regardless of how many books each author actually has (the average of 5 books per author doesn't change the query COUNT, only the row count each of those 200 queries returns). Total: 1 (findAll) + 200 (one per author) = 201 queries -- the textbook N+1 shape, where N is the number of parent rows whose lazy collection gets touched.

findByCountry, as originally written, issues one query to fetch matching authors, but leaves each one's books collection as an unfetched LAZY proxy. The stream's a.getBooks().size() call then forces Hibernate to resolve that proxy separately for every single author in the result -- exactly the N+1 pattern, invisible with a few local test rows but severe once the country filter matches thousands of authors in production. Adding @EntityGraph(attributePaths = "books") to the same derived method tells Spring Data JPA to eagerly fetch the books association as part of the SAME query used to find authors by country, populating every returned author's books collection immediately -- so by the time the stream's .map() runs, no author's books collection is still a lazy, unresolved proxy, and the extra per-author queries disappear entirely. The derived method's name and behavior are otherwise unchanged; only the fetching strategy for this specific query was fixed.

code:
# Request 1: no credentials supplied at all
GET /api/admin/reports HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.com

# Response: 401 Unauthorized
# -- Spring Security has no idea who is making this request at all.


# Request 2: valid credentials for a real, authenticated user -- but that
# user only has ROLE_CUSTOMER, and this endpoint requires ROLE_ADMIN
GET /api/admin/reports HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.com
Authorization: Basic YW15OnBhc3N3b3JkMTIz

# Response: 403 Forbidden
# -- Spring Security knows exactly who this is; that identity is simply
# not permitted to access this specific resource.

exp: Request A returns 401 Unauthorized, because no credentials were supplied at all -- the server cannot establish any identity, so authentication itself fails before an authorization decision is even possible. Request B returns 403 Forbidden, because the credentials ARE valid and correspond to a real, known user (authentication succeeds), but that user's granted authorities (ROLE_CUSTOMER) don't satisfy this endpoint's requirement of ROLE_ADMIN, so the request is correctly denied at the authorization stage instead.
code:
// Request A
GET /api/admin/audit-log HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.com

// Request B
GET /api/admin/audit-log HTTP/1.1
Host: api.example.com
Authorization: Basic <valid credentials for a ROLE_CUSTOMER user>
expl: The two requests fail at two different, sequential stages of the filter chain. Request A never even reaches an authorization decision, because there's no credential to authenticate in the first place -- the authentication stage itself fails, and Spring Security's exception-translation filter converts that into 401 Unauthorized, the standard response for 'you have not established who you are.' Request B's credentials ARE valid, so the authentication stage succeeds and a real Authentication object, with ROLE_CUSTOMER among its granted authorities, is placed into the SecurityContext for this request. The authorization stage then runs next, checks that authority list against this endpoint's requirement (ROLE_ADMIN), finds no match, and denies the request -- resulting in 403 Forbidden, the standard response for 'you are known, but not permitted to do this.' The distinction matters in practice because a client encountering 401 knows it needs to (re-)authenticate, while a client encountering 403 knows re-authenticating as the SAME user won't help at all -- a fundamentally different signal to act on.

This is Spring Boot's intended, fail-safe default: the moment spring-boot-starter-security is on the classpath, its security autoconfiguration activates and locks down EVERY endpoint behind authentication by default, creates a single in-memory user named 'user' with a randomly generated password (printed once, in the startup logs, specifically so someone can actually log in and confirm security really is active), and rejects any unauthenticated request with 401. This is deliberate: Spring Boot would rather an entire application become suddenly, loudly inaccessible the moment security is added than have a team assume 'we added the dependency, so we must be secure now' while some endpoint stays accidentally, silently open. Nothing is actually broken -- the team simply hasn't yet written the configuration that declares which endpoints, like /api/health, should be genuinely public. The real fix is to define a SecurityFilterChain bean using HttpSecurity that explicitly marks specific paths as permitAll() and leaves (or explicitly marks) the rest as requiring authentication -- replacing the blanket default lockdown with a deliberate, reviewable policy, which is exactly the subject of the next concept.

anyRequest() matches literally every request by definition, and because it was declared FIRST, Spring Security's first-match-wins evaluation stops right there for every single request, including ones under /api/public/** -- the permitAll() and hasRole("ADMIN") rules declared afterward are structurally unreachable, since no request can ever fail to match anyRequest() and 'fall through' to them. This is why GET /api/public/status was incorrectly requiring authentication: it matched anyRequest().authenticated() before it ever got a chance to match the intended permitAll() rule. Moving the specific rules ahead of the catch-all, and keeping anyRequest() last, restores the intended behavior: a request to /api/public/** now matches that specific, permissive rule first, before the broader authenticated() rule is ever considered.

@PreAuthorize is inert without @EnableMethodSecurity present on some @Configuration class -- Spring only wraps beans in the AOP proxy responsible for evaluating method-security annotations when explicitly told to via @EnableMethodSecurity, and SecurityConfig here never declared it. Because the proxy was never created, getAllReports() ran exactly like any ordinary, unguarded method for every caller, regardless of role, which is exactly why a non-admin user's manual test call succeeded. Adding @EnableMethodSecurity to SecurityConfig instructs Spring to create that proxy around ReportService (and every other bean with method-security annotations), so calls to getAllReports() are now actually intercepted and evaluated against the current Authentication's granted authorities before the real method body ever executes -- correctly rejecting a caller without ROLE_ADMIN going forward.

The original code calls passwordEncoder.encode(rawPassword) fresh, on every login attempt, which generates a brand-new random salt each time -- completely unrelated to whatever salt was embedded in the hash stored at registration. Comparing that freshly-generated hash against the stored one with .equals() will essentially always return false, since two BCrypt hashes of the same password produced with two different random salts look nothing alike, regardless of whether the entered password is correct. The fix replaces this with passwordEncoder.matches(rawPassword, user.getHashedPassword()), which correctly extracts the salt already embedded in the STORED hash, re-hashes the candidate rawPassword using that exact same salt, and only then compares -- which is the only mechanism that can correctly verify a password without ever needing the original raw password to have been retained anywhere.

exp: attackerCheck is (almost certainly) false, because encode("correcthorse") called a second time generates a brand-new, unrelated random salt, producing a hash string that looks nothing like storedHash even though the underlying password is identical. loginCheck is true, because matches(...) extracts the salt already embedded in storedHash itself and re-hashes "correcthorse" using that exact same salt before comparing, which correctly confirms the password matches regardless of what a fresh, independently-salted encode() call would produce.
expl: The attacker's approach fundamentally misunderstands what BCrypt guarantees: encode("correcthorse") does not produce a stable, repeatable 'fingerprint' of the string "correcthorse" -- it produces a hash tied to whatever fresh, random salt happens to be generated on that particular call, and two separate calls to encode() with the identical input produce two different salts and therefore two different-looking hash strings almost every single time. Comparing the attacker's freshly-generated hash to storedHash with .equals() is comparing two hashes built from two unrelated salts, so it fails regardless of whether the underlying password is correct -- this is precisely why a stolen hash database can't be attacked by simply re-hashing guesses and directly comparing the resulting strings. The real login flow avoids this entirely by using matches(rawPassword, storedHash), which reads the salt that's already embedded directly inside storedHash (this is exactly what BCrypt's own hash format is designed to make possible) and re-hashes the candidate password using that identical salt before comparing -- the only correct way to verify a BCrypt-hashed password, and the reason PasswordEncoder exposes matches() as a distinct method rather than expecting callers to compare two encode() outputs directly.

@WebMvcTest scans and registers only the web layer -- @Controller/@RestController beans, plus supporting web infrastructure -- and explicitly excludes @Service and @Repository beans from component scanning. Because no OrderService bean is ever registered in this context, @Autowired has nothing to find and the context fails to start while trying to construct OrderController, whose constructor demands an OrderService. Replacing @Autowired with @MockBean fixes this correctly: rather than looking for an existing bean, @MockBean creates a Mockito mock and registers IT as the OrderService bean in this test's context, which satisfies OrderController's constructor while keeping the real service (and everything it would otherwise depend on) out of the picture entirely.

exp: Both assertions pass: firstTestPersistsAnItem sees count() == 1 right after persisting one item, and secondTestSeesAnEmptyTable sees count() == 0, because @DataJpaTest automatically rolls back each test method's transaction once that method completes -- the widget persisted in the first test never actually commits, so the second test starts from a genuinely empty table.
expl: @DataJpaTest wraps every individual test method in its own database transaction, and by default rolls that transaction back automatically once the method finishes -- regardless of whether the test passed or failed. In firstTestPersistsAnItem, entityManager.persist(...) adds a row within that method's transaction, so inventoryRepository.count() correctly reports 1 while still inside that same transaction. Once the method returns, Spring's test framework rolls the transaction back, which erases that insert as if it never happened. secondTestSeesAnEmptyTable then runs in a brand new transaction with no knowledge of the first test's data at all, so count() correctly reports 0. This automatic rollback is precisely why @DataJpaTest tests can run in any order and be repeated indefinitely without ever needing explicit teardown code to reset the database between them.

The original request supplies a body via .content(...) but never declares a Content-Type at all. Without a declared Content-Type, Spring MVC has no way to select which HttpMessageConverter should be responsible for reading that body, and the @RequestBody parameter resolution fails before the controller's own logic (and therefore before any JSON structure or validation issue) is ever considered -- producing 415 Unsupported Media Type, a transport-level rejection, not a data problem. Adding .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON) declares the body's format explicitly, letting Spring MVC correctly select the Jackson-based JSON converter, after which deserialization and the rest of the request proceeds normally.

given(productService.findById(5L)).willReturn(...) stubs the mocked ProductService so that, when the controller calls it with 5L (extracted from the {id} path variable in the request), it returns a fully-populated Product rather than null or a default mock response. mockMvc.perform(get("/api/products/5")) sends the simulated request through the real DispatcherServlet and HandlerMapping, which routes it to ProductController's handler method, binds 5 from the path to the Long parameter, and calls the (mocked) service. The response, serialized by the real Jackson converter, is then asserted field by field with jsonPath -- confirming both the status code and that the controller correctly passed the service's data through into the JSON response body.

The request in this test hits GET /api/orders/1, which causes the controller to call orderService.findById(1L) -- but the stub was written for findById(2L), a completely different, unstubbed call as far as Mockito is concerned. Because Mockito's default behavior for an unstubbed call is to silently return null rather than throw or warn, orderService.findById(1L) returned null, and the controller's own attempt to call .getCustomerName() on that null Order threw the NullPointerException the test actually observed -- nowhere near the assertion lines, which never even got a chance to run. Changing the stub to findById(1L) (matching the actual request) makes the mock respond correctly to the call the controller genuinely makes, letting the rest of the test run and assert as intended.

exp: count is 0 (int's default), name is null (String is a reference type with no stubbing), inStock is false (boolean's default), and tags is an empty List (Mockito's smart default for common collection return types) -- none of these calls throw, because Mockito's default answer for an unstubbed mock method is a lenient, type-appropriate default value, not an exception.
code:
// No when(...)/given(...) stubbing has been set up for inventoryService at all.

Integer count = inventoryService.getStockCount("WIDGET");     // int return type
String name = inventoryService.getProductName("WIDGET");      // String return type
boolean inStock = inventoryService.isInStock("WIDGET");        // boolean return type
List<String> tags = inventoryService.getTags("WIDGET");        // List<String> return type
expl: Mockito assigns a default 'answer' to every mock method that hasn't been explicitly stubbed, and that default depends entirely on the method's declared return type. For primitive numeric and boolean return types, the default is the type's natural zero-equivalent -- 0 for getStockCount's int, false for isInStock's boolean -- because a primitive can't be null and Mockito has to return something. For an ordinary reference type like String, with no special-cased default behavior, the answer is null. For well-known collection interfaces like List, Set, and Map, Mockito's default answer (RETURNS_DEFAULTS, which delegates to ReturnsEmptyValues) specifically returns an empty, non-null collection rather than null, precisely to reduce a common and easy-to-hit source of NullPointerExceptions when calling .size() or iterating over an unstubbed collection result. None of these calls throw an exception at all, which is exactly the behavior worth internalizing: a genuinely unanticipated call to a @MockBean fails silently and by returning something plausible-looking, not loudly.
